questions.title: How do I determine whether to review the Board's likelihood-of-confusion findings de novo or for substantial evidence?
questions.question_body: I am trying to understand the standard of review applied in this case. The opinion states on page 2 that the court reviews the Board's legal conclusions de novo but its findings of fact for substantial evidence. However, the DuPont factors are described as both 'findings of relevant underlying facts' and 'questions of law.' Can someone clarify the interactive relationship between these two standards when analyzing the DuPont factors?

questions.title: Does a dictionary definition alone justify a finding that 'banking' and 'credit card services' are legally identical under the Second DuPont factor?
questions.question_body: Apex argues in its brief that it is a retail bank not a credit card issuer, yet the Board ruled their services were 'legally identical, in part' based on dictionary definitions for 'banking' and 'finance' extending credit. I'm confused about how relying on dictionary definitions can overcome the factual reality that Apex didn't currently offer credit cards and CC Serve didn't issue them either, but rather serviced accounts for banks. Is this a precedent for how the Board handles service similarity, or did they overlook the actual business model?

questions.title: Why did the Board incorrectly limit the 'relevant public' solely to consumers of credit card services in its analysis of the Sixth DuPont factor?
questions.question_body: The court vacated the Board's finding on the sixth DuPont factor because it felt the 'relevant public' should match the scope found in the second factor. In the second factor, services were deemed 'highly similar' and 'partially legally identical.' If they are legally identical regarding the relevant public, why couldn't the Board consider the 42 other third-party marks using 'Aspire' in the broader banking and financing sector? Isn't it standard to define 'similar goods' narrowly to avoid irrelevant comparisons in crowded markets?

questions.title: What is the specific evidentiary threshold for a mark to be considered 'ubiquitous' or 'considerable' under the Sixth DuPont factor?
questions.question_body: Under Juices Generation and Jack Wolfskin, there are different standards for marking marks as 'considerable' or 'ubiquitous.' In this case, the Board found 9 'notable' marks were not enough to show considerable use. The court on appeal notes there were '42 other third-party marks.' Based on the pre-emption calling 26 marks 'considerable' in Juices Generation, can someone explain how the court determines if a specific number (or set of examples) of third-party registrations reaches the threshold of 'sufficient commercial strength' to be ignored or considered 'ubiquitous' as a distraction?

questions.title: Why did the court vacate the First DuPont factor analysis simply because of an error in the Sixth DuPont factor?
questions.question_body: The First DuPont factor looks at the similarity of the marks (appearance, sound, connotation). The Sixth DuPont factor looks at crowded markets. The court says 'Because commercial impression informs the analysis under the first DuPont factor, we must similarly vacate the Board's analysis here.' Can someone explain the doctrinal logic here? Does the presence of too many similar marks (Sixth Factor) automatically mean a mark has a 'weak commercial impression' (First Factor)? How is that causal link established?
